779:   const sendMessage = useCallback(
780:     async (
781:       text: string,
782:       attachments: ChatAttachmentPayload[] = [],
783:       options: { from?: string } = {},
784:     ) => {
785:       const trimmed = text.trim();
786:       if ((!trimmed && !attachments.length) || streaming) {
787:         return;
788:       }
789: 
790:       // A re-ask replaces the turn it starts from: the old question and the
791:       // answer it got are the same turn, and keeping both would read as a
792:       // conversation the reader never had.
793:       const cut = options.from
794:         ? messages.findIndex((message) => message.id === options.from)
795:         : -1;
796:       const replaced = cut >= 0 ? messages.slice(0, cut) : messages;
797: 
798:       // Files ride only on the newest turn. Re-sending megabytes of base64 with
799:       // every later question would make each turn slower than the last.
800:       const history: ChatMessage[] = [
801:         ...replaced.map((message) =>
802:           message.attachments
803:             ? {
804:                 id: message.id,
805:                 role: message.role,
806:                 content: message.content,
807:                 parts: message.parts,
808:               }
809:             : message,
810:         ),
811:         {
812:           role: "user",
813:           id: newTurnId(),
814:           content: trimmed,
815:           ...(attachments.length ? { attachments } : {}),
816:         },
817:       ];
818:       const assistantIndex = history.length;
819:       const assistantId = newTurnId();
820:       setMessages([
821:         ...history,
822:         { role: "assistant", id: assistantId, content: "", parts: [] },
823:       ]);
824:       setStreaming(true);
825:       setThinkingPhase("health_check");
826:       setOfflineReply(false);
827: 
828:       const controller = new AbortController();
829:       abortRef.current = controller;
830: 
831:       let content = "";
832:       let parts: ChatPart[] = [];
833:       let steps: RunStep[] = [];
834:       let failure: StudioError | null = null;
835:       let terminal = false;
836:       let stopped = false;
837: 
838:       // Prose is appended to the open text part; a surface opens a new one, so
839:       // the transcript keeps the agent's order instead of gathering all prose
840:       // above all cards.
841:       const appendText = (text: string) => {
842:         if (!text) {
843:           return;
844:         }
845:         content += text;
846:         const last = parts[parts.length - 1];
847:         parts =
848:           last?.kind === "text"
849:             ? [...parts.slice(0, -1), { kind: "text", text: last.text + text }]
850:             : [...parts, { kind: "text", text }];
851:       };
852: 
853:       // The turn owns its own timeline, so a finished run stays inspectable and
854:       // the next turn starts from nothing without a reset elsewhere.
855:       const publish = () => {
856:         setMessages((prev) => {
857:           if (prev.length <= assistantIndex) {
858:             return prev;
859:           }
860:           const next = [...prev];
861:           next[assistantIndex] = {
862:             role: "assistant",
863:             id: assistantId,
864:             content,
865:             parts: [...parts],
866:             ...(failure ? { error: failure, retryText: trimmed } : {}),
867:             ...(stopped ? { stopped: true, retryText: trimmed } : {}),
868:             ...(failure || stopped
869:               ? attachments.length
870:                 ? { retryAttachments: attachments }
871:                 : {}
872:               : {}),
873:             ...(steps.length ? { tools: [...steps] } : {}),
874:           };
875:           return next;
876:         });
877:       };
878: 
879:       const handleEvent = (event: RawSseEvent) => {
880:         switch (event.event) {
881:           case "status": {
882:             const phase = String(event.data.phase ?? "");
883:             setThinkingPhase(phase);
884:             if (phase === "offline") {
885:               setOfflineReply(true);
886:             }
887:             break;
888:           }
889:           case "delta": {
890:             appendText(String(event.data.text ?? ""));
891:             publish();
892:             break;
893:           }
894:           case "ui": {
895:             // Validate again on arrival: the connection is local but the
896:             // renderer must never trust a shape it has not checked.
897:             const parsed = parseUiSpec(event.data.spec, catalogManifest());
898:             if (parsed.ok) {
899:               parts = [
900:                 ...parts,
901:                 { kind: "ui", id: String(event.data.id ?? `ui-${parts.length}`), node: parsed.node },
902:               ];
903:               publish();
904:             }
905:             break;
906:           }
907:           case "tool":
908:             steps = applyToolEvent(
909:               steps,
910:               {
911:                 name: String(event.data.name ?? ""),
912:                 status: String(event.data.status ?? ""),
913:                 preview: event.data.preview ? String(event.data.preview) : undefined,
914:               },
915:               Date.now(),
916:             );
917:             publish();
918:             break;
919:           case "message": {
920:             terminal = true;
921:             content = String(event.data.content ?? content);
922:             const hasSurfaces = parts.some((part) => part.kind === "ui");
923:             if (!hasSurfaces) {
924:               parts = content ? [{ kind: "text", text: content }] : [];
925:             }
926:             publish();
927:             break;
928:           }
929:           case "conversation": {
930:             const id = String(event.data.id ?? "");
931:             if (id) {
932:               setConversationId(id);
933:             }
934:             break;
935:           }
936:           case "memory": {
937:             const observation = event.data.observation as Observation | undefined;
938:             if (observation?.id) {
939:               setMemory((prev) =>
940:                 prev.some((item) => item.id === observation.id)
941:                   ? prev.map((item) => (item.id === observation.id ? observation : item))
942:                   : [...prev, observation],
943:               );
944:             }
945:             break;
946:           }
947:           case "canvas_dirty":
948:             void refreshCanvas();
949:             break;
950:           case "connector": {
951:             if (String(event.data.status ?? "") === "error") {
952:               const reason = String(event.data.error ?? "The connector could not be added.");
953:               setMessages((prev) => [
954:                 ...prev,
955:                 { role: "notice", id: newTurnId(), content: `Connector failed: ${reason}` },
956:               ]);
957:             } else {
958:               setConnectorSuggestions((prev) => {
959:                 const id = String(event.data?.preset ?? event.data?.name ?? "");
960:                 if (!id || prev.includes(id)) {
961:                   return prev;
962:                 }
963:                 return [...prev, id];
964:               });
965:             }
966:             void refreshConnectors();
967:             break;
968:           }
969:           case "error": {
970:             terminal = true;
971:             failure = readStudioError(event.data.error);
972:             publish();
973:             break;
974:           }
975:           default:
976:             break;
977:         }
978:       };
979: 
980:       try {
981:         await streamChat(
982:           {
983:             base_url: settings.base_url,
984:             api_key: settings.api_key,
985:             model: settings.model_name,
986:             mcp_url: settings.mcp_url,
987:             messages: history,
988:             brief,
989:             ui_catalog: catalogManifest(),
990:             conversation_id: conversationId,
991:           },
992:           handleEvent,
993:           controller.signal,
994:         );
995:       } catch (error) {
996:         const aborted = (error as Error).name === "AbortError";
997:         if (aborted) {
998:           // An abort is the user's own doing, so it is not a failure — but it is
999:           // still a fact about the turn. Keep what arrived, stop any tool that
1000:           // was mid-flight, and leave the turn in place so the transcript says
1001:           // what happened instead of silently losing the question.
1002:           stopped = true;
1003:           steps = steps.map((step) =>
1004:             step.status === "running"
1005:               ? {
1006:                   ...step,

83: /** A tool name as a phrase a person would say, e.g. "Reading your jobs". */
84: export function stepLabel(name: string): string {
85:   const known = TOOL_LABELS[name];
86:   if (known) {
87:     return known;
88:   }
89:   const humanized = name.replace(/[_-]+/g, " ").trim();
90:   return humanized || "Using a tool";
91: }
92: 
93: function lastOpenStep(steps: RunStep[], name: string): number {
94:   for (let index = steps.length - 1; index >= 0; index -= 1) {
95:     const step = steps[index];
96:     if (step.status === "running" && step.name === name) {
97:       return index;
98:     }
99:   }
100:   return -1;
101: }
102: 
103: /**
104:  * Fold one `tool` event into the timeline.
105:  *
106:  * A `start` opens a step; `ok`/`error` resolves the newest open step with that
107:  * name. A result with no matching start (a replayed stream, a client that
108:  * joined late) becomes a finished step rather than being dropped.
109:  */
110: export function applyToolEvent(steps: RunStep[], event: ToolEvent, now: number): RunStep[] {
111:   const name = event.name.trim() || "tool";
112: 
113:   if (event.status === "start") {
114:     return [
115:       ...steps,
116:       {
117:         id: `${name}-${steps.length}`,
118:         name,
119:         status: "running",
120:         startedAt: now,
121:       },
122:     ];
123:   }
124: 
125:   const status: RunStepStatus = event.status === "error" ? "error" : "ok";
126:   const open = lastOpenStep(steps, name);
127:   if (open === -1) {
128:     return [
129:       ...steps,
130:       {
131:         id: `${name}-${steps.length}`,
132:         name,
133:         status,
134:         preview: event.preview,
135:         startedAt: now,
136:         endedAt: now,
137:       },
138:     ];
139:   }
140: 
141:   return steps.map((step, index) =>
142:     index === open
143:       ? { ...step, status, preview: event.preview ?? step.preview, endedAt: now }
144:       : step,
145:   );
146: }
147: 
148: /** Durations are read at a glance, so they stay to one short form. */
149: export function formatDuration(ms: number): string {
150:   if (!Number.isFinite(ms) || ms < 0) {
151:     return "0s";
152:   }
153:   if (ms < 1000) {
154:     return `${(ms / 1000).toFixed(1)}s`;
155:   }
156:   if (ms < 60_000) {
157:     const seconds = ms / 1000;
158:     return `${seconds < 10 ? seconds.toFixed(1) : Math.round(seconds)}s`;
159:   }
160:   const minutes = Math.floor(ms / 60_000);
161:   const seconds = Math.round((ms % 60_000) / 1000);
162:   return `${minutes}m ${seconds}s`;
163: }
164: 
165: /** The step still in flight, if the run has one. */
166: export function runningStep(steps: RunStep[]): RunStep | null {
167:   for (let index = steps.length - 1; index >= 0; index -= 1) {
168:     if (steps[index].status === "running") {
169:       return steps[index];
170:     }
171:   }
172:   return null;
173: }
174: 
175: /**
176:  * What the studio is doing right now: the tool it is waiting on, or the phase
177:  * it is in. Deliberately about work, never about the model's reasoning.
178:  */
179: export function activityLabel(phase: string | null, steps: RunStep[]): string {
180:   const running = runningStep(steps);
181:   if (running) {
182:     return stepLabel(running.name);
183:   }
184:   return (phase ? PHASE_LABELS[phase] : undefined) ?? "Thinking";
185: }
186: 
187: /**
188:  * The one line a finished run leaves behind. Counts and time only: the point is
189:  * that work happened, not a replay of every call.
190:  */
191: export function runSummary(steps: RunStep[], now: number): string {
192:   if (!steps.length) {
193:     return "";
194:   }
195:   const started = Math.min(...steps.map((step) => step.startedAt));
196:   const ended = Math.max(...steps.map((step) => step.endedAt ?? now));
197:   const failures = steps.filter((step) => step.status === "error").length;
198:   const parts = [`${steps.length} tool${steps.length === 1 ? "" : "s"}`];
199:   if (failures) {
200:     parts.push(`${failures} failed`);
201:   }
202:   parts.push(formatDuration(ended - started));
203:   return parts.join(" · ");
204: }

This is very revealing. The `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` branch represents a significant evolution of the assistant-ui integration. It includes:

**Backend changes (studio-api):**
1. New `approvals.py` module - for tool approval flows
2. `chat.py` changes:
   - `MUTATING_TOOL_PREFIXES` - identifies tools that need approval
   - `is_mutating_tool()` - check function
   - `MAX_ATTACHMENTS`, `MAX_ATTACHMENT_TEXT`, `MAX_SOURCE_PREVIEW`
   - Tool approval flow with `wait_for_decision`
   - Source references (provenance chips)
   - Attachment refs instead of embedded base64
3. `schemas.py` changes:
   - `ChatAttachment` → `AttachmentRef` (client-side file handling, text extraction by client)
   - `ChatRequest` has `approvals`, `assistant_id` fields
   - `ApprovalDecisionRequest`/`ApprovalDecisionResponse`
   - `TurnNode` for conversation tree (branching)
   - `ConversationModel` has `head_id` for branch positioning
   - `TurnModel` has `message_id`, `parent_id`
   - `ConversationTreeResponse` - full branch tree
   - `UpdateConversationRequest` - for updating head_id

**Frontend changes (studio):**
1. `StudioRuntime.tsx` - Full provider with all handlers
2. `convert.ts` - Bidirectional conversion with reasoning, sources, tool approvals
3. `parts.tsx` - Part renderers using assistant-ui's scoped state
4. `ThreadComposer.tsx` and `composerParts.tsx` - Assistant-ui composer
5. `attachments.ts` - Attachment adapter for assistant-ui

**Our branch (`ui-not-looking-like-shit`) has:**
1. Simplified `Conversation.tsx` with inlined runtime
2. `lib/thread.ts` with simplified conversion (no reasoning, sources, tool approvals)
3. `ChatStage.tsx` handles attachments directly
4. No branching, no tool approvals

So the "crash" seems to be that our branch was an earlier, simpler attempt at the assistant-ui integration, and the `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` branch represents the more complete "max" version.

Now, the user wants us to "pick up from where we left off" to "ensure assistant-ui is installed and used to the max." This means we need to bring the full assistant-ui capabilities from `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` into our branch.

But wait - the user said "we had a crash" and we need to "pick up from where we left off on this topic branch." This suggests our branch IS the current state of work, and we need to continue building on it.

            "tool_call_id": self.tool_call_id,
            "name": self.name,
            "arguments": self.arguments,
            "prompt": self.prompt,
            "created_at": self.created_at,
        }

class ApprovalDecision:
    approved: bool
    reason: str = ""

    """No pending gate has that id, or it already resolved."""

    """Pending approval gates, keyed by the id the client answers with."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._pending: dict[str, asyncio.Future[ApprovalDecision]] = {}

    def open(
        self,
        *,
        tool_call_id: str,
        name: str,
        arguments: dict[str, object],
        prompt: str,
    ) -> tuple[ApprovalRequest, asyncio.Future[ApprovalDecision]]:

        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()

            name=name,
            arguments=arguments,
            prompt=prompt,

        with self._lock:
            self._pending[request.id] = future
        return request, future

        with self._lock:
            self._pending.pop(approval_id, None)

    def cancel_all(self) -> None:
        """Drop every pending gate. Called when the sidecar shuts down."""
        with self._lock:
            pending = list(self._pending.items())
            self._pending.clear()

            if not future.done():
                future.cancel()

    def pending(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return len(self._pending)


async def wait_for_decision(
    registry: ApprovalRegistry,
    request: ApprovalRequest,
    future: asyncio.Future[ApprovalDecision],
    timeout: float = DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
) -> ApprovalDecision | None:
    """Await a decision, returning ``None`` when the gate expired or was dropped.

    The gate is always discarded, so an expired id can never be answered later
    and a cancelled turn leaves nothing behind.
    """

    except asyncio.TimeoutError:

    except asyncio.CancelledError:

    "ApprovalDecision",
    "ApprovalNotFoundError",
    "ApprovalRegistry",
    "ApprovalRequest",
    "DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS",
    "wait_for_decision",
]

"""Conversational helper with offline fallbacks and a streaming tool loop.

The loop fans the MCP tools and three local tools — ``render_ui``,
``remember``, and ``add_connector`` — into the completion. Local tools are
intercepted rather than forwarded: ``render_ui`` validates its spec against the
catalog the client sent and streams a ``ui`` event, ``remember`` stores a
suggested observation and streams a ``memory`` event, and ``add_connector``
writes the shared connector registry and streams a ``connector`` event.

The conversation is persisted when a memory store is supplied, so a PM can leave
and come back to the same thread and the same working context.
"""

Now I can see the key differences in schemas:

**Our branch (current):**
- `ChatAttachment` with `name`, `media_type`, `data` (base64) - server-side decoding
- `ChatMessage` with `role`, `content`, `attachments` (inline) - no `id`, no `parent_id`
- `ChatRequest` without `attachments` field and without `approvals`/`assistant_id`
- `ModelsRequest` (not `ModelListRequest`)

**feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience:**
- `AttachmentRef` with `name`, `content_type`, `size`, `text` (client-extracted), `data_url` (for images)
- `ChatMessage` with `role`, `content`, `id`, `parent_id` (for branching)
- `ChatRequest` with `attachments: list[AttachmentRef]`, `approvals: bool`, `assistant_id: str | None`
- `ModelListRequest` (not `ModelsRequest`)
- `ApprovalDecisionRequest`/`ApprovalDecisionResponse`
- `TurnNode`, `ConversationTreeResponse`, `UpdateConversationRequest` for branching

The key difference is that the feature branch moved attachment processing to the client side (client extracts text, server just gets text/data_url), and added support for:
1. Tool approvals (mutating tools need user confirmation)
2. Branching/conversation threads
3. Reasoning (chain-of-thought)
4. Source references (provenance)
5. Client-side attachment handling

This is a very significant divergence. Our branch (`ui-not-looking-like-shit`) has a simpler, working integration, but the `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` branch represents the "max" use of assistant-ui with all capabilities.

"""Pydantic request/response contracts for the Living Studio sidecar API."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ChatAttachment(BaseModel):
    """One file the reader attached, as bytes the sidecar can decode.

    ``data`` is base64. Images become image content; text is inlined verbatim.
    The sidecar decides which, from ``media_type``, and refuses the rest rather
    than letting a filename stand in for content the model never saw.
    """

    name: str = ""
    media_type: str = ""
    data: str = ""


class ChatMessage(BaseModel):
    role: Literal["system", "user", "assistant", "tool"]
    content: str = ""
    attachments: list[ChatAttachment] = Field(default_factory=list)


class McpHealthRequest(BaseModel):
    mcp_url: str


class LlmHealthRequest(BaseModel):
    base_url: str
    api_key: str = ""
    model: str = ""


class ModelsRequest(BaseModel):
    base_url: str
    api_key: str = ""


class AddStepRequest(BaseModel):
    mcp_url: str
    job_id: str
    name: str
    order: int


class AddOutcomeRequest(BaseModel):
    mcp_url: str
    job_id: str
    statement: str
    importance: float
    satisfaction: float


class CreateJobRequest(BaseModel):
    """Create a Job by hand, with or without the model."""

    name: str = Field(min_length=1)
    description: str | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class UpdateJobRequest(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class UpdateStepRequest(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    order: int | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class UpdateOutcomeRequest(BaseModel):
    statement: str | None = None
    importance: float | None = None
    satisfaction: float | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class StudioBrief(BaseModel):
    """The user's context, captured during first-run onboarding."""

    product_name: str = ""
    product_url: str = ""
    target_user: str = ""
    job_statement: str = ""
    core_problem: str = ""


class UiCatalogRequest(BaseModel):
    """What the calling client can render. Omitted by non-visual clients."""

    version: int = 1
    components: list[dict[str, Any]] = Field(default_factory=list)


class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    base_url: str
    api_key: str = ""
    model: str
    mcp_url: str
    messages: list[ChatMessage] = Field(default_factory=list)
    brief: StudioBrief | None = None
    ui_catalog: UiCatalogRequest | None = None
    conversation_id: str | None = None


class AddConnectorRequest(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    preset: str | None = None
    url: str | None = None


class ConnectorListItem(BaseModel):
    name: str
    kind: str
    enabled: bool = True


class ConnectorOperationResponse(BaseModel):
    ok: bool
    name: str


ObservationKind = Literal[
    "career",
    "opportunity",
    "business",
    "stakeholder",
    "constraint",
    "evidence",
    "preference",
]
ObservationStatus = Literal["suggested", "confirmed", "dismissed"]


class ObservationModel(BaseModel):
    id: str
    kind: str
    text: str
    data: dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    status: str
    confidence: float
    source_turn: int | None = None
    created_at: str
    updated_at: str


class ObservationListResponse(BaseModel):
    observations: list[ObservationModel]


class ObservationResponse(BaseModel):
    observation: ObservationModel


class ObservationCreateRequest(BaseModel):
    kind: ObservationKind
    text: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=2000)
    data: dict[str, Any] | None = None
    confidence: float = Field(default=0.6, ge=0, le=1)
    confirmed: bool = False


class ObservationUpdateRequest(BaseModel):
    text: str | None = Field(default=None, min_length=1, max_length=2000)
    status: ObservationStatus | None = None
    data: dict[str, Any] | None = None
    confidence: float | None = Field(default=None, ge=0, le=1)


class ConversationModel(BaseModel):
    id: str
    title: str
    created_at: str
    updated_at: str


class ConversationResponse(BaseModel):
    conversation: ConversationModel


class TurnModel(BaseModel):
    id: int
    conversation_id: str
    role: str
    content: str
    created_at: str


class LatestConversationResponse(BaseModel):
    conversation: ConversationModel | None = None
    turns: list[TurnModel] = Field(default_factory=list)

1: /**
2:  * Files the reader hands the studio.
3:  *
4:  * A file is only worth attaching if the model can actually read it, so the same
5:  * rules the sidecar enforces are applied here first, in words the reader can act
6:  * on. Nothing is ever sent as a filename alone: the bytes travel with the turn.
7:  */
8: 
9: import type { ChatAttachmentPayload } from "../types";
10: 
11: /** One turn's upload must stay bounded; base64 adds a third to every byte. */
12: export const MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024;
13: export const MAX_ATTACHMENTS = 6;
14: 
15: /** Text-bearing types with no `text/` prefix that are still safe to inline. */
16: export const INLINE_MEDIA_TYPES = new Set([
17:   "application/json",
18:   "application/xml",
19:   "application/yaml",
20:   "application/x-yaml",
21:   "application/toml",
22:   "application/csv",
23:   "application/x-ndjson",
24:   "application/sql",
25: ]);
26: 
27: /** A file waiting to be sent, with what the transcript needs to show it. */
28: export interface StagedAttachment extends ChatAttachmentPayload {
29:   id: string;
30:   size: number;
31:   /** An object URL for an image, so the reader can check it before sending. */
32:   preview_url?: string;
33: }
34: 
35: export function mediaTypeOf(file: { type: string }): string {
36:   return (file.type || "").split(";")[0].trim().toLowerCase();
37: }
38: 
39: export function isImage(attachment: { media_type: string }): boolean {
40:   return (attachment.media_type || "").split(";")[0].trim().toLowerCase().startsWith("image/");
41: }
42: 
43: export function isReadable(file: { type: string }): boolean {
44:   const media = mediaTypeOf(file);
45:   return media.startsWith("image/") || media.startsWith("text/") || INLINE_MEDIA_TYPES.has(media);
46: }
47: 
48: /**
49:  * Why this file cannot be attached, or null when it can. `staged` is how many
50:  * files are already waiting, so the count limit is enforced before reading.
51:  */
52: export function attachmentProblem(
53:   file: { name: string; type: string; size: number },
54:   staged: number,
55: ): string | null {
56:   if (staged >= MAX_ATTACHMENTS) {
57:     return `Attach up to ${MAX_ATTACHMENTS} files at a time.`;
58:   }
59:   if (!isReadable(file)) {
60:     const media = mediaTypeOf(file) || "unknown";
61:     return `${file.name} is ${media === "unknown" ? "an untyped file" : `a ${media} file`}. Attach an image or a text file.`;
62:   }
63:   if (file.size === 0) {
64:     return `${file.name} is empty.`;
65:   }
66:   if (file.size > MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES) {
67:     return `${file.name} is larger than ${MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES / (1024 * 1024)} MB.`;
68:   }
69:   return null;
70: }
71: 
72: let sequence = 0;
73: 
74: /**
75:  * Read a file into the shape the sidecar expects: base64 bytes plus the media
76:  * type, never a path. Images keep an object URL for the preview; the caller owns
77:  * revoking it.
78:  */
79: export function readAttachment(file: File): Promise<StagedAttachment> {
80:   return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
81:     const reader = new FileReader();
82:     reader.onerror = () => reject(new Error(`Could not read ${file.name}.`));
83:     reader.onload = () => {
84:       const result = String(reader.result ?? "");
85:       const comma = result.indexOf(",");
86:       const data = comma === -1 ? "" : result.slice(comma + 1);
87:       if (!data) {
88:         reject(new Error(`Could not read ${file.name}.`));
89:         return;
90:       }
91:       sequence += 1;
92:       const media_type = mediaTypeOf(file);
93:       resolve({
94:         id: `${file.name}-${file.lastModified}-${sequence}`,
95:         name: file.name,
96:         media_type,
97:         data,
98:         size: file.size,
99:         ...(media_type.startsWith("image/") ? { preview_url: URL.createObjectURL(file) } : {}),
100:       });
101:     };
102:     reader.readAsDataURL(file);
103:   });
104: }
105: 
106: /** Drop the preview, and nothing else, when a staged file leaves the tray. */
107: export function releaseAttachment(attachment: StagedAttachment): void {
108:   if (attachment.preview_url) {
109:     URL.revokeObjectURL(attachment.preview_url);
110:   }
111: }
112: 
113: /** What goes on the wire: no ids, no previews, no sizes. */
114: export function toPayload(attachment: StagedAttachment): ChatAttachmentPayload {
115:   return {
116:     name: attachment.name,
117:     media_type: attachment.media_type,
118:     data: attachment.data,
119:   };
120: }
121: 
122: /** A short, human size for a chip. */
123: export function formatBytes(bytes: number): string {
124:   if (bytes < 1024) {
125:     return `${bytes} B`;
126:   }
127:   if (bytes < 1024 * 1024) {
128:     return `${Math.round(bytes / 1024)} KB`;
129:   }
130:   return `${(bytes / (1024 * 1024)).toFixed(1)} MB`;
131: }

## Summary of Current State

### Our branch (`ui-not-looking-like-shit`) - Current State
Has a **simplified assistant-ui integration**:

- `lib/thread.ts` has conversion functions (`toThreadMessage`, `textOf`, `turnFromAppend`, `metaOf`) - simple, no reasoning/sources/approvals
- `lib/attachments.ts` has `StagedAttachment`/`ChatAttachmentPayload` (base64 data) - client reads files and sends bytes
- `ChatStage.tsx` handles attachments through `sendMessage(text, attachments)` directly
- No branching, no tool approvals, no reasoning display
- No `StudioRuntime.tsx` provider wrapper
- All tests pass, typecheck passes
- Backend: `ChatAttachment` (base64), `ChatMessage` without `id`/`parent_id`, no approvals infrastructure, no `AttachmentRef`, no conversation tree API

### `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` - The "Max" Target
Has a **full assistant-ui integration**:
- `StudioRuntime.tsx` wraps the entire app with `AssistantRuntimeProvider` at the app root
- `assistant/convert.ts` - Rich bidirectional conversion with reasoning, sources, tool approvals, `toChatMessage` inverse
- `assistant/parts.tsx` - Part renderers: `ReasoningPart`, `SourcePart`, `SurfacePart`, `ToolPart` with approval UI, `TypingPart`, `AssistantAvatar`
- `assistant/attachments.ts` - Full attachment adapter (`createAttachmentAdapter`, `preparedAttachments`), `AttachmentRef` type (client-side text extraction)
- `ThreadComposer.tsx` + `composerParts.tsx` - Using `ComposerPrimitive` from assistant-ui
- `Conversation.tsx` uses `MessagePrimitive`, `BranchPickerPrimitive`, `MessagePrimitive.Parts` with component registration
- Types: `ChatAttachment` (with `id`, `contentType`, `size`, `text`, `dataUrl`), `ChatPart` with `reasoning`, `tool` (with `approval`), `source`, `ChatMessage` with `parentId`, `ToolStatus`, `ToolApproval`
- StudioContext has `regenerateFrom`, `editFrom`, `switchBranch`, `respondToApproval`
- Backend: `ApprovalRegistry` + `approvals.py`, `AttachmentRef` schema, reasoning events, source events, approval events, conversation tree API, `CAPABILITIES` from core

# Agentic ODI - AI Developer Guardrails

This file provides system instructions and guardrails for any AI agents (or LLMs) assisting with the development of the **Agentic ODI** project. Please adhere to these guidelines to maintain consistency and align with the project's vision.

> **Source of Truth for ODI Methodology**: `docs/reference/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` by Anthony W. Ulwick (Strategyn). All ODI concepts in this project are grounded in that document. When in doubt, refer agents back to its definitions.

---

## 🎯 ODI Methodology Guardrails

This section defines how agents MUST understand and apply Outcome-Driven Innovation within this project. These are not implementation guidelines — they are domain constraints that ensure the system reflects the ODI methodology correctly.

### What is Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)?

ODI is a strategy and innovation process rooted in the **Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)** theory. Its core premise is: **people buy products and services to get a "job" done**. A "job" is the functional process a person is trying to execute — it remains stable over time, while products and technologies are point-in-time solutions that eventually become obsolete.

ODI achieves an **86% innovation success rate** by replacing guesswork with a rigorous, data-driven framework grounded in measurable customer needs.

---

### Stage 1: Define the Market and the Job-to-be-Done

- A **market** is defined as: **a group of people + the functional job they are trying to get done** (e.g., "parents trying to pass on life lessons to children").
- A **Job-to-be-Done** is the core functional unit of analysis. It is NOT a product, solution, or feature — it is a stable human goal.
- **Agent rule**: Before anything else, the agent MUST help the user define the Job-to-be-Done. If no Job exists, use `add_job` to capture it. If one exists already, use `get_jobs()` to check first.
- ❌ **Never skip this stage**. No outcomes, steps, or scoring can be meaningful without a well-defined Job.

---

### Stage 2: Uncover Desired Outcomes

- **Desired outcomes** are the metrics customers use to measure success when getting a job done. They are the "needs" in ODI.
- Qualitative interviews typically uncover **50–150 desired outcome statements**.
- **Correct outcome statement format** (must be enforced when capturing user input):

  > `[Direction] + [Unit of Measure] + [Object of Control] + [Contextual Clarifier]`

  - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the time it takes to determine if the corn seeds are germinating."*
  - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the likelihood of damaging the surface when cutting."*
  - ❌ **Bad**: *"Make it faster"* — too vague, no direction, no measurable unit.
  - ❌ **Bad**: *"I want a notification"* — this is a solution/feature, not an outcome.

- **Agent rule**: Guide the user to express outcomes using this exact format. Reject or reframe vague statements before calling `add_outcome`. Always capture `importance` and `satisfaction` scores (1–10 scale) to enable opportunity scoring.

---

### Stage 3: Inventory the Job (Universal Job Map)

- All functional jobs decompose into **8 universal process steps** (the Universal Job Map):
  1. **Define** — Plan what needs to be done; select goals or resources
  2. **Locate** — Gather the inputs, information, or resources needed
  3. **Prepare** — Set up and organize everything required
  4. **Confirm** — Validate readiness; decide whether to proceed
  5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
  6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
  7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
  8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs

- **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
- ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.

---

### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)

- Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
  - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
  - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?

- **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):

  ```
  Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
  ```

- **Interpretation**:
  - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
  - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
  - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.

# Testing

## Commands

```bash
uv run pytest                       # all packages + root contract/launcher tests
uv run pytest packages/core         # one package
uv run pytest tests/contract        # MCP contract only
uv run mypy apps packages tests
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r apps packages
```

The root `pyproject.toml` owns pytest, coverage, ruff, mypy, and bandit configuration. There is no per-package test configuration to keep in sync.

## Layout

Tests live next to their package (`packages/*/tests`, `apps/*/tests`). Root `tests/` contains only cross-package checks:

- `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py` — live FastMCP names, argument names, and required fields match `agentic_odi_core.contract.TOOL_SPECS`.
- `tests/contract/test_cli_contract.py` — the CLI local-handler keys are a subset of `TOOL_NAMES`.
- `tests/scripts/` — dev launcher helpers and lifecycle.

- Use `InMemoryRepository` in tests. `create_app(InMemoryRepository())` keeps the Studio API off the real `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`.
- The MCP server uses `build_repository()`; tests set `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:` before import and call tools through `Client(mcp)` without HTTP.
- Async tests use `@pytest.mark.asyncio` (strict mode).

CI runs the root suite on Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12, collects coverage for every `agentic_odi_*` distribution, and uploads `coverage.xml` from the 3.12 job. <skill_content name="writing-plans">
# Skill: writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

# Max Studio Assistant-UI Integration Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Bring the `ui-not-looking-like-shit` branch to the full "max" assistant-ui integration represented by `feat/studio-assistant-ui-existence` — adding backend approval gates, conversation branching, reasoning/source/tool-part streaming, and a complete frontend `assistant/` module with runtime provider, rich message conversion, part rendering, and attachment adapters.

**Architecture:** Adopt the reference branch's approach wholesale: an `assistant/StudioRuntime.tsx` wraps the app with `AssistantRuntimeProvider`; `assistant/convert.ts` does bidirectional Studio↔assistant-ui message conversion with reasoning, sources, tool approvals, and attachments; `assistant/parts.tsx` renders each part kind; `ThreadComposer.tsx` replaces `Composer.tsx`; `StudioContext` gains branching and approval methods; the backend gains `approvals.py`, conversation tree memory, and event-stream reasoning/source/approval emission.

**Tech Stack:** FastAPI + SQLite (studio-api), React + TypeScript + `@assistant-ui/react@0.15.31` (studio SPA), Vitest + pytest.

**Spec:** `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` branch — the reference implementation. All file contents and test expectations are read from this branch.

## Global Constraints

- Keep `@assistant-ui/react@^0.15.31` (already pinned in `apps/studio/package.json`).
- Python 3.10+; async tests decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`.
- Use `InMemoryRepository` + `create_app(InMemoryRepository())` in API tests; never touch real `~/.agentic-odi/studio.db`.
- Frontend: `npm --prefix apps/studio test -- --run` for Vitest; `npm --prefix apps/studio run typecheck` for tsc.
- All Python: `uv run ruff check .` and `uv run ruff format --check .` must pass.
- `uv run mypy apps packages` must pass.

## Review Focus

| Input / Condition | Expected Behavior |
|---|---|
| Assistant emits a `reasoning` delta in the SSE stream | Renders in `ReasoningPart`, hidden by default, expandable. |
| Assistant calls a write tool without `requires_approval` flag | No approval gate; tool runs directly. |
| Assistant calls a write tool with `requires_approval` flag | Stream emits `approval` event; turn pauses; UI shows approval prompt. |
| User accepts or declines approval | `PATCH /api/approvals/{id}` with `approved` + `reason`; turn resumes or ends. |
| User asks a follow-up question after a tool result | New turn has the tool result as a `source`; model sees full visible history. |
| Image attachment > 5 MB | Rejected client-side with human-readable message. |
| Legacy conversation rows (no `message_id`/`parent_id`) | Read as a linear chain; head = last row. |
| User switches branches | Head updates; subsequent turns branch from the selected ancestor. |
| `content` field arrives on a part we don't map | Dropped; other parts preserved for history. |

# Max Studio Assistant-UI Integration Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Bring the `ui-not-looking-like-shit` branch to the full "max" assistant-ui integration represented by `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` — adding backend approval gates, conversation branching, reasoning/source/tool-part streaming, and a complete frontend `assistant/` module with runtime provider, rich message conversion, part rendering, and attachment adapters.

**Architecture:** Adopt the reference branch's approach wholesale: an `assistant/StudioRuntime.tsx` wraps the app with `AssistantRuntimeProvider`; `assistant/convert.ts` does bidirectional Studio↔assistant-ui message conversion with reasoning, sources, tool approvals, and attachments; `assistant/parts.tsx` renders each part kind; `ThreadComposer.tsx` replaces `Composer.tsx`; `StudioContext` gains branching and approval methods; the backend gains `approvals.py`, conversation tree memory, and event-stream reasoning/source/approval emission.

**Tech Stack:** FastAPI + SQLite (studio-api), React + TypeScript + `@assistant-ui/react@0.15.31` (studio SPA), Vitest + pytest.

**Spec:** `feat/studio-assistant-ui-experience` branch — the reference implementation. All file contents and test expectations are read from this branch.

## Global Constraints

- Keep `@assistant-ui/react@^0.15.31` (already pinned in `apps/studio/package.json`).
- Python 3.10+; async tests decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`.
- Use `InMemoryRepository` + `create_app(InMemoryRepository())` in API tests; never touch real `~/.agentic-odi/studio.db`.
- Frontend: `npm --prefix apps/studio test -- --run` for Vitest; `npm --prefix apps/studio run typecheck` for tsc.
- All Python: `uv run ruff check .` and `uv run ruff format --check .` must pass.
- `uv run mypy apps packages` must pass.

## Review Focus

| Input / Condition | Expected Behavior |
|---|---|
| Assistant emits a `reasoning` delta in the SSE stream | Renders in `ReasoningPart`, hidden by default, expandable. |
| Assistant calls a write tool without `requires_approval` flag | No approval gate; tool runs directly. |
| Assistant calls a write tool with `requires_approval` flag | Stream emits `approval` event; turn pauses; UI shows approval prompt. |
| User accepts or declines approval | `PATCH /api/approvals/{id}` with `approved` + `reason`; turn resumes or ends. |
| User asks a follow-up question after a tool result | New turn has the tool result as a `source`; model sees full visible history. |
| Image attachment > 5 MB | Rejected client-side with human-readable message. |
| Legacy conversation rows (no `message_id`/`parent_id`) | Read as a linear chain; head = last row. |
| User switches branches | Head updates; subsequent turns branch from the selected ancestor. |
| `content` field arrives on a part we don't map | Dropped; other parts preserved for history. |

---

Tasks are ordered by dependency: **Backend first** (API, schemas, memory, approvals), then **Frontend types**, then **Frontend assistant module**, then **Component wiring**, then **Tests**, finally **Docs**.

+"""In-process approval gates for mutating tool calls.
+
+A mutating MCP tool (``add_job``, ``update_outcome``, …) pauses the streaming
+turn until the person in front of the Studio says yes or no. The gate is a
+process-local registry of pending futures: the SSE generator awaits one, and
+``POST /api/approvals/{id}`` resolves it.
+
+This is deliberately the smallest thing that is honest. The sidecar serves one
+local user over one loopback socket; it has no durable job state and no worker
+pool, so a gate that lives in memory is the whole requirement. Every gate has a
+timeout and every gate resolves once, so a turn can never hang and a double
+click can never run a tool twice.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import asyncio
+import threading
+import uuid
+from dataclasses import dataclass, field
+from datetime import datetime, timezone
+
+#: A person deciding whether the agent may write to their data deserves longer
+#: than a network timeout, but the turn must still end on its own.
+DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 300.0
+
+
+@dataclass
+class ApprovalRequest:
+    """One pending decision, described well enough for the UI to ask."""
+
+    id: str
+    tool_call_id: str
+    name: str
+    arguments: dict[str, object]
+    prompt: str
+    created_at: str = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat())
+
+    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, object]:
+        return {
+            "id": self.id,
+            "tool_call_id": self.tool_call_id,
+            "name": self.name,
+            "arguments": self.arguments,
+            "prompt": self.prompt,
+            "created_at": self.created_at,
+        }
+
+
+@dataclass
+class ApprovalDecision:
+    approved: bool
+    reason: str = ""
+
+
+class ApprovalNotFoundError(KeyError):
+    """No pending gate has that id, or it already resolved."""
+
+
+class ApprovalRegistry:
+    """Pending approval gates, keyed by the id the client answers with."""
+
+    def __init__(self) -> None:
+        self._lock = threading.Lock()
+        self._pending: dict[str, asyncio.Future[ApprovalDecision]] = {}
+
+    def open(
+        self,
+        *,
+        tool_call_id: str,
+        name: str,
+        arguments: dict[str, object],
+        prompt: str,
+    ) -> tuple[ApprovalRequest, asyncio.Future[ApprovalDecision]]:
+        """Register a gate and return its description and the future to await."""
+        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
+        request = ApprovalRequest(
+            id=f"apv_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}",
+            tool_call_id=tool_call_id,
+            name=name,
+            arguments=arguments,
+            prompt=prompt,
+        )
+        future: asyncio.Future[ApprovalDecision] = loop.create_future()
+        with self._lock:
+            self._pending[request.id] = future
+        return request, future
+
+    def resolve(self, approval_id: str, decision: ApprovalDecision) -> None:
+        """Answer a pending gate. Raises when the gate is unknown or already closed."""
+        with self._lock:
+            future = self._pending.pop(approval_id, None)
+        if future is None or future.done():
+            raise ApprovalNotFoundError(approval_id)
+        future.set_result(decision)
+
+    def discard(self, approval_id: str) -> None:
+        """Forget a gate without answering it (the turn ended first)."""
+        with self._lock:
+            self._pending.pop(approval_id, None)
+
+    def cancel_all(self) -> None:
+        """Drop every pending gate. Called when the sidecar shuts down."""
+        with self._lock:
+            pending = list(self._pending.items())
+            self._pending.clear()
+        for _approval_id, future in pending:
+            if not future.done():
+                future.cancel()
+
+    @property
+    def pending(self) -> int:
+        with self._lock:
+            return len(self._pending)
+
+
+async def wait_for_decision(
+    registry: ApprovalRegistry,
+    request: ApprovalRequest,
+    future: asyncio.Future[ApprovalDecision],
+    timeout: float = DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
+) -> ApprovalDecision | None:
+    """Await a decision, returning ``None`` when the gate expired or was dropped.
+
+    The gate is always discarded, so an expired id can never be answered later
+    and a cancelled turn leaves nothing behind.
+    """
+    try:
+        return await asyncio.wait_for(future, timeout=timeout)
+    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
+        return None
+    except asyncio.CancelledError:
+        raise
+    finally:
+        registry.discard(request.id)
+
+
+__all__ = [
+    "ApprovalDecision",
+    "ApprovalNotFoundError",
+    "ApprovalRegistry",
+    "ApprovalRequest",
+    "DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS",
+    "wait_for_decision",
+]

 def _apply_add_connector(
     arguments: dict[str, Any], service: ConnectorService
 ) -> tuple[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
     """Register a connector locally and return SSE event dicts for the stream."""
     name = arguments.get("name")
     preset_id = arguments.get("preset")
     url = arguments.get("url")
     try:
         config = service.add(name=name, preset_id=preset_id, url=url)
     except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
         event = {"event": "connector", "data": {"status": "error", "error": str(exc)}}
         return f"Error: {exc}", [event]
     event_data: dict[str, Any] = {"action": "registered", "name": config.name}
     if preset_id is not None:
         event_data["preset"] = preset_id
     if url is not None:
         event_data["url"] = url
     return f"registered connector {config.name}", [{"event": "connector", "data": event_data}]
 
 
 def _apply_remember(
     arguments: dict[str, Any], memory: StudioMemory | None
 ) -> tuple[str, dict[str, Any] | None]:
     """Store one suggested observation without asking the PM first."""
     if memory is None:
         return "Memory is not available to this client.", None
 
     kind = str(arguments.get("kind", ""))
     text = str(arguments.get("text", ""))
     data = arguments.get("data")
     try:
         confidence = float(arguments.get("confidence", 0.6))
     except (TypeError, ValueError):
         confidence = 0.6
 
     try:
         observation = memory.add_observation(
             kind=kind,
             text=text,
             data=data if isinstance(data, dict) else None,
             status="suggested",
             confidence=confidence,
         )
     except ValueError as exc:
         return f"Could not remember that: {exc}", None
     return "Saved for the user to review.", {"observation": observation.to_dict()}

     cleaned = text.strip()

     if len(cleaned) > MAX_TEXT:

     return value

+def _chunk(

+    tool_calls: list[Any] | None = None,

+    return SimpleNamespace(choices=[SimpleNamespace(delta=delta)])

+def _parse(frames: list[str]) -> list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]]:
+    events: list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]] = []
+    for frame in frames:

+        data = None
+        for line in frame.splitlines():
+            if line.startswith("event: "):
+                name = line[len("event: ") :]
+            elif line.startswith("data: "):

# Skill: subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (under `<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down
what you checked as you check it:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks
that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against
what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether
its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it
specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan
is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran.

Write the table to the ledger. Rule on everything you find before execution
begins — each finding against the plan text that mandates it — and record
each ruling in the ledger. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment.

plan is its argument — record the ruling beside its row, and dispatch

implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in

  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.

  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into

  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
